analysis.one_liner: Requires regular government inspections of food processing plants and gives regulators mandatory recall power over contaminated food.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in April 1999 and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required every facility that processes or handles food for American consumers to register with the government, put safety controls in place, and open its doors to unannounced inspections at least four times a year. It would have let the Health and Human Services Secretary order mandatory recalls of contaminated food, fine violators up to $100,000 per violation, protect whistleblowers, and set up a system to verify the safety of imported food. The Senate Agriculture Committee never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, who face millions of foodborne illnesses each year. The bill would have required quarterly unannounced inspections of food plants, mandatory registration, contamination tolerances based on risks to children and other sensitive groups, mandatory recalls of dangerous products, civil fines, whistleblower protection for employees who report violations, and a citizen right to sue violators or an agency that fails to do its job [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires every food processing and handling facility, including importers' facilities, to register annually with HHS, and allows suspension of registration — which stops all commerce from that facility — for refusing inspections or committing food-law violations [S3].

Mandates unannounced inspections at least quarterly for most facilities, with standards for classifying low-risk facilities, and gives inspectors authority to impound and condemn products found in violation [S3][S2].

Amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to require notification of suspected violations and to authorize voluntary and, when companies refuse, mandatory recalls with consumer notification [S3][S2].
Allows civil penalties of up to $100,000 per act, with each day of a continuing violation a separate offense, and prohibits retaliation against employees who report food-safety violations [S3][S2].

Requires a comprehensive import-safety system with routine inspection of foreign facilities and ports of entry, and lets anyone sue violators or the Secretary for failing to perform mandatory duties [S3][S2].

analysis.who_pays: Food processors, handlers, and importers, who would bear the cost of registration, process controls, recordkeeping, sampling, and more frequent inspections. Taxpayers would fund the expanded inspection, surveillance, research, and state-assistance programs, since the bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' for fiscal years 2000 and 2001 [S3][S2].

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for registration, process controls, recordkeeping, and frequent inspections would fall on food processors and could be passed to consumers as higher prices, and the burden falls hardest on smaller operators without in-house compliance staff [S3].

Quarterly inspections of nearly all registered facilities is a large expansion of government inspection capacity; the bill authorizes open-ended appropriations, so its cost to taxpayers was left entirely to the annual spending process [S3].

The citizen-suit provision allows anyone to sue violators or the Secretary over nondiscretionary duties, with attorney's fees and penalties available, which critics would call an invitation to litigation [S3].
The bill excludes pesticide residues and food additives already regulated under specific FDCA provisions from its contaminant tolerances, leaving those regimes untouched [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is straightforward: stronger government oversight of food processing in exchange for compliance costs that would partly show up in food prices and partly in federal spending. The safeguards — mandatory recalls, penalties, whistleblower protection, citizen suits — were real and aimed at a problem (foodborne illness) that sickens millions of Americans a year. The main design weakness is that it left funding open-ended and imposed a uniform quarterly inspection schedule, softened only by a low-risk exemption the Secretary would have had to define.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in April 1999, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001 [S5][S1].

narrative.text: Sen. Byron Dorgan introduced the bill on April 28, 1999, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S5][S1].
Two Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
No further action — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the record after the referral, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food processors, handlers, and importers came out ahead: they avoided quarterly inspections, registration, mandatory recall authority, civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation, and citizen lawsuits. Consumers did not get the added food-safety protections.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters — the sponsor and two cosponsors — were Democrats, and the Republican-run Agriculture Committee took no action on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have imposed registration, process controls, recordkeeping, quarterly unannounced inspections, and civil penalties of up to $100,000 per act on these facilities. Their compliance cost was the public's safety gain.

The bill required importers to register their foreign facilities, subjected imports to inspection at ports of entry and abroad, and barred entry of products that appear to violate food-safety law, with registration suspension as the remedy for violating foreign facilities.
The bill authorized new funding, staffing-scale inspection duties, cooperation agreements with states, and research and surveillance programs run through HHS and CDC.
